title: Integer Promotion, Unsigned Conversion and Wrap
quickIdea: C converts operands before it combines them. Narrow types are promoted to int, and the moment one operand is unsigned the other is converted to unsigned too, so a difference that should be negative becomes a huge positive number.
remember: Integer promotion: char, signed char, unsigned char, short and unsigned short are converted to int (or to unsigned int when int cannot hold all their values) before any arithmetic. So 'a' + 1 is int arithmetic.
Usual arithmetic conversions: if either operand is unsigned int, the other is converted to unsigned int and the result is unsigned. A wider unsigned type wins over a narrower one.
size_t is unsigned, and strlen returns size_t. So strlen(a) - strlen(b) is computed modulo 2^32 (or 2^64) and is never negative.
Unsigned overflow wraps modulo 2^n, and that is defined behaviour. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so a program that overflows a signed int has no required output at all.
signed char c = 200; stores 200 - 256 = -56 in 8-bit two's complement, while unsigned char keeps 200. The bits are identical; the interpretation is not.
Integer division truncates toward zero: 7 / 2 is 3 and -7 / 2 is -3. Converting to float after the division is too late.

example.prompt: char *x = "abc", *y = "defgh"; unsigned int c = 0; int len = ((strlen(x) - strlen(y)) > c) ? strlen(x) : strlen(y); printf("%d", len); What is printed?
example.work: strlen(x) is 3 and strlen(y) is 5, both of type size_t. Their difference is computed in unsigned arithmetic, so 3 - 5 wraps to 2^32 - 2, a very large number. Comparing that with c = 0 is true, so the conditional selects strlen(x), which is 3, and len holds 3.
example.answer: 3. The comparison was never '3 > 0 against -2'; it was a huge unsigned value against 0.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2017 Set 1 Q.53 is this program and the printed value is 3. The same rule decides any question that compares strlen results, subtracts two sizeof values, or tests i < strlen(s) after i has gone negative.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: int i = -1; unsigned int u = 1; what does printf("%d", i < u) print?
variations.answer: 0 - i is converted to unsigned (UINT_MAX) before the comparison, so -1 < 1 is false.
variations.why: The same conversion as the 2017 question with the polarity reversed, which catches a student who memorised 'the difference wraps' instead of the rule.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is signed overflow undefined behaviour while unsigned overflow is merely wrap-around?
variations.answer: The standard specifies unsigned arithmetic as arithmetic modulo 2^n, so the result is defined; for signed types it imposes no requirement at all, so a compiler may assume overflow never happens and optimise on that assumption.
variations.why: Explains why an overflowing signed counter has no answer to trace, which some loop questions quietly rely on.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: int a = 7, b = 2; float r = a / b; printf("%f", r); what is printed?
variations.answer: 3.000000 - the division is integer division because both operands are int, and the conversion to float happens at the assignment.
variations.why: The truncate-before-convert trap from the same family of one-mark questions; (float)a / b would give 3.5.

trap.what: Comparing a signed difference against an unsigned zero.
trap.why: Once one side of the comparison is unsigned, the signed side is converted to unsigned. A difference of -2 becomes 2^n - 2, so 'is the first string shorter?' answers yes for every pair of lengths.
trap.counterexample: With strlen("abc") - strlen("defgh") the difference is -2 mathematically, but (strlen("abc") - strlen("defgh")) > 0 is true, because the left side is the unsigned value 4294967294 on a 32-bit int.

check.question: What does the expression (strlen("ab") - strlen("abc")) > 0 evaluate to?
check.explanation: 2 - 3 in size_t arithmetic wraps to SIZE_MAX, which is greater than 0. The mathematical answer -1 never appears.
